summary: Describes a modification to TCP congestion control that decays the congestion window after a long period when the application had little to send, using the slow-start threshold to remember the earlier window. It was experimental and is now historic, replaced by RFC 7661.

plainLanguage.summary: If you stop sending for a while, the network may have changed. TCP is told to start more carefully instead of rushing back to its old speed.

questions: what happens to cwnd when idle
subtitle: Remembering what the network could carry after a TCP connection goes idle.

tldr.problem: When a TCP sender stops transmitting for a while (idle or application-limited), the congestion window becomes unreliable: the network may have changed, and the window no longer reflects current capacity. If the sender then resumes at full speed, it may overwhelm the network.
tldr.mechanism: TCP Congestion Window Validation (CWV) decays the congestion window by half for every round-trip time the flow remains idle. It saves the pre-idle window size in ssthresh so the sender can recover quickly using slow-start once data arrives again.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2861 was experimental and has been superseded by RFC 7661. Most modern TCP implementations take different approaches, though the core principle—validating that old window estimates remain accurate—is now a recognized concern in TCP design.

facts.label: Decay rate
facts.value: Half the congestion window per RTO

today: RFC 2861 is Historic as of RFC 7661. Modern TCP implementations use different congestion window validation strategies that are often integrated with their broader congestion control algorithms. However, the concern it raised—that idle or application-limited periods invalidate congestion window estimates—remains a recognized problem in TCP design.

sections.title: Why Congestion Windows Become Stale
sections.content:
TCP's congestion window (cwnd) grows as the sender successfully transmits data, and shrinks when loss is detected. In steady state, a sender sending constantly has up-to-date knowledge of the path: every transmitted segment is either delivered or lost, revalidating the window size. But when a TCP sender becomes idle or application-limited—sending fewer bytes than the window allows—this revalidation stops. The network may have changed; other flows may have consumed the available capacity. The old congestion window is no longer reliable.

Most TCP implementations at the time had no strategy for this, or simply reused the old window after an idle period. RFC 2581 suggested slow-start after very long idle periods, but left a gap for shorter or partial-idle scenarios. RFC 2861 proposes a solution: decay the window based on how long the sender has been inactive or application-limited.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you know a hallway is 10 people wide. You take a break for an hour. When you come back, you don't know if the hallway still holds 10 people—maybe everyone left, maybe crowds arrived. TCP needs to check carefully before assuming it can use the old capacity.

sections.title: Congestion Window Validation Algorithm
sections.content:
RFC 2861 defines two scenarios. First, complete idle: if the sender has not sent any packet for more than one round-trip time (RTO), then before sending the next packet, it halves cwnd for every RTO of idleness. Second, application-limited: the sender has data but is not filling the window (because the application is slow or the receiver is slow). In this case, the sender should not grow cwnd when it receives acknowledgments, because the old window was never fully utilized.

The algorithm uses slow-start threshold (ssthresh) as memory. When cwnd is reduced, ssthresh is set to at least 3/4 of the old cwnd. This allows the sender to quickly slow-start (exponential growth) back toward its previous rate once the sender becomes network-limited again, without overshooting.

Two key variables track state: T_prev (last time the window was revalidated by a full transmission) and W_used (the maximum unacknowledged data sent during the application-limited period). When the sender goes idle for more than RTO seconds, cwnd is halved repeatedly. When application-limited for more than RTO, cwnd is set to (cwnd + W_used) / 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm has two parts: first, if you stopped sending entirely, shrink your window before starting again. Second, if you're sending slowly (not filling your window), don't let your window grow, because you never used the space you already had.

sections.title: Implementation Details and Pseudocode
sections.content:
The RFC includes pseudocode for implementations. When TCP sends a data segment, it first checks: has more than RTO time elapsed since the last segment? If yes, the sender has been idle. Set ssthresh to max(ssthresh, 3/4 cwnd), then halve cwnd once for each RTO that has passed. Reset tracking variables T_prev and W_used.

After sending, TCP checks: did this segment fill the advertised congestion window? If yes, the sender is network-limited, and the window is revalidated. Set T_prev to now, and W_used to zero. If the segment did not fill the window and the send queue is empty, then the sender is application-limited. Track the maximum unacknowledged data in W_used. If more than RTO has elapsed since the last revalidation, reduce cwnd to (cwnd + W_used) / 2, update ssthresh, and reset T_prev and W_used.

The result is that during periods when the sender is idle or application-limited, cwnd decays roughly once per RTO (one round-trip time). The use of RTO as the trigger means implementations need only check at packet-send time, not maintain background timers.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a packet, look at the clock. If it's been a while since your last packet, shrink your window. If you're sending slowly, don't let the window grow when you get confirmations back.

sections.title: Validation and Current Status
sections.content:
RFC 2861 validates the algorithm through simulations in the NS network simulator and experiments on FreeBSD. One real-world test used an SSH connection over a modem link. With CWV, the connection avoided a burst of retransmissions when the user suddenly listed a large file, resulting in roughly 30% faster transfer. Another test over a real dialup ppp link showed that CWV produced smoother, better-behaved flow without large bursts.

However, RFC 2861 was marked Experimental, and RFC 7661 eventually replaced it. Modern TCP implementations have adopted different strategies for handling idle or application-limited periods, often integrating congestion window validation into broader congestion control algorithms. The core insight—that stale congestion windows need decay—remains relevant, though the specific algorithm here is no longer the standard solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests showed it worked: connections behaved better and avoided packet loss. But the approach was experimental, and newer ideas have since taken over.

left.title: Completely Idle

right.title: Application-Limited
right.desc: Packets sent, but fewer than the window allows.
